summary: An excerpt from a fiction book (Book 1, part 100) in which a teacher, Ms Galvez, tells a class about 1960s-70s San Francisco radicals such as the Yippies, including Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak as university dropouts. The narrator, drawn to the story, asks whether the Yippies won, and Ms Galvez argues they changed the world by ending the Vietnam War and advancing civil rights. Charles objects strongly, calling them terrorists, and Ms Galvez points out they were American citizens, leading to his angry outburst that the country was at war and they were giving aid to the enemy.
one_line: A classroom debate in a fiction novel over whether 1960s radicals like the Yippies were heroes or terrorists, and whether they won.
key_facts: Ms Galvez says San Francisco was ground zero for the movement in which the kids of the day were taking to the streets, dropping out, and freaking out.
Ms Galvez says revolutionary armies were founded in San Francisco and some blew up buildings or robbed banks for their cause.
Ms Galvez names Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak as university dropouts who founded Apple Computers and invented the PC.
When asked whether the Yippies won, Ms Galvez says "They didn't lose," and that they "kind of imploded a little."
Ms Galvez says some Yippies went to jail for drugs or other things, while others became yuppies and told everyone how stupid they had been.
Ms Galvez claims the Yippies changed the world: the war in Vietnam ended and unquestioning obedience once called patriotism went out of style.
Ms Galvez says Black rights, women's rights, and gay rights came a long way, and that Chicano rights and rights for disabled people were created or strengthened by these people.
Ms Galvez states that today's protest movement is the direct descendant of those struggles.
Charles says "I can't believe you're talking about them like this" and his face goes red as he leans forward, half standing.
Charles says the Yippies are actual terrorists who blew up buildings, tried to destroy the stock exchange, and beat up cops.
Charles exclaims "They attacked us!" in reaction to the Yippies' actions.
Ms Galvez responds that the Yippies weren't foreign agents but American citizens, and asks who "they" and "us" are.
Charles shouts "Crap!" and says the country was at war then and these people were giving aid and comfort to the enemy.
The narrator says that the street demonstrations, which had once seemed lame, now seemed less lame, and that there might be room for that kind of action in the Xnet movement.
